edge.title: The other party who is always interested
edge.setup: A broker shows you a flat. Before you've reached the lift, there's a call about another family deciding tonight, and the owner may raise the quote tomorrow. You're asked for a token amount to 'hold' it — ₹25,000, adjustable later.
edge.tell: A deadline you can't verify, created by a person paid on commission.
move: Token money is almost never genuinely refundable, whatever is said aloud. Treat it as spent.
Say: 'If it goes, it goes.' Watch what happens to the deadline — real urgency survives this; manufactured urgency dissolves.
Ask for the owner's number and talk directly. Brokers resist this precisely because the pressure lives in the gap between you.
edge.why: A broker is paid for a transaction closing, not for you choosing well. That isn't villainy, it's structure — and once you see the structure, 'another party is interested' stops reading as information and starts reading as a job being done.
edge.variants: Same shape: car dealers' 'this EMI scheme ends today', gym joining fees waived 'only this month', insurance agents' quarter-end calls.

lens.name: Compounding
lens.one_line: Small consistent changes beat big sporadic ones, because the result is multiplicative, not additive.
lens.detail: Intuition is linear; compounding isn't, which is why almost everyone underestimates it. ₹5,000 a month at 12% is about ₹11 lakh in 10 years and roughly ₹50 lakh in 20 — most of that gain arriving in the final stretch. The same shape governs skills, reputation and debt. Credit-card interest at 3.5% a month is this force running against you at roughly 50% a year.
elsewhere: Minimum card payments keeping a balance alive for years.
Reputation: slow to build, then suddenly everything arrives at once.
lens.test: Is this a one-time event, or something that multiplies? Multiplying things deserve disproportionate attention.
lens.today: Deccan Herald reports Dasara-rush motorists stranded for six hours, and the Times of India has long-distance buses crawling out of Bengaluru until 2.30 am on Friday night. A jam like this is not a steady loss: everyone who leaves late joins a queue that grows faster than it clears, so each delayed departure adds to the delay of the next. The practical reading is that the first 30 minutes of a bad start cost far more than 30 minutes by the end of the night, so leave well before the peak rather than 'a little early'.

moved.what: Dasara rush left Bengaluru motorists stranded for six hours (Deccan Herald), and long-distance buses crawled out of the city until 2.30 am on Friday night (Times of India). A chemical-laden truck also caught fire on the NICE road, halting traffic (The Hindu).
moved.so_what: If you travel out of the city this week, leave before the evening peak, not just a little earlier, and avoid the NICE road until it is clear; check live traffic before you start.

moved.what: Bengaluru cab fares crossed ₹100 per km in rain and traffic, with no guarantee of a ride (Times of India, Urban Acres). Festival airfares have also surged to ₹35,000 (India Business Trade).
moved.so_what: With rain forecast again, book your return ride or flight before you need it and keep the Metro as a fallback; do not plan a tight connection that depends on finding a cab.

moved.what: Joint owners of a Bengaluru property can now split an A-eKhata online and get separate records (Times of India).
moved.so_what: If you co-own a flat or site, you can apply online for your own khata record instead of sharing one document, which makes selling or borrowing against your share simpler.

moved.what: Anyone who missed the Gruha Jyothi survey should visit the nearest Escom office by 31 October (Times of India).
moved.so_what: If you were away when the survey happened, go before 31 October rather than risk a problem with your free-power benefit.

moved.what: Bengaluru schools and colleges with polling booths will be closed on 22 and 23 October for council elections (Times of India).
moved.so_what: Check your child's school or college circular today and plan childcare or study arrangements for those two days.

carry_over.prompt: You are in a packed festival ground and have only noticed the gate you came in by. What single check tells you that you are standing in a bottleneck?
carry_over.answer: If you cannot point to two exits without crossing the thickest part of the crowd, you are standing in a bottleneck.
